newsitem.title: UK: UK unemployment falls to five-year low, earnings up.
newsitem.headline: UK unemployment falls to five-year low, earnings up.

text.p: British unemployment has tumbled to its lowest level in more than five years but wage inflation ticked higher, a slew of economic figures showed on Wednesday.
A total of 35,600 people were taken off the jobless queues in September, figures from the Office for National Statistics showed -- the largest monthly fall since December 1994.
That took the overall unemployment rate down to 7.4 percent and the total number of jobless, at 2.073 million, to its lowest level since February 1991.
Good news for the unemployed was matched by a boost for those in work. The ONS revised up annual average earnings growth to 4.0 percent in July, from 3.75, and said it held at that level in August.

UK employment minister Eric Forth said the government remained relaxed about wage inflation, despite the pick-up in average earnings. He noted earnings growth has stuck between three and four percent for about three years now.
The opposition Labour Party said 95 percent of new jobs are part-time and the number of full-time employees fell by 47,000 over the summer.

Economists were concerned by the data, not least since September's Public Sector Borrowing Requirement -- the gap between government spending and revenue -- totalled 3.41 billion pounds ($5.41 billion), overshooting market forecasts of a 2.7 billion shortfall.
The PSBR figures were released alongside the jobs data.
"The labour data is worrying, showing signs of strengthening demand for labour feeding through to labour costs," said Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse Tilney.
"It belies the theory that inflation might be dead."
Underlying retail price inflation edged up to 2.9 percent year-on-year in September, sticking stubbornly above the government's 2.5 percent target.
